title: DATE vs DATEVALUE: build a date or parse one
meta_desc: DATE vs DATEVALUE: DATE assembles a date from year/month/day numbers; DATEVALUE parses a date written as text. When each is the right tool, plus locale gotchas.
intro: Both hand you a real date value, but from opposite starting points. DATE builds one from separate year, month, and day NUMBERS. DATEVALUE parses one out of a TEXT string that looks like a date. If your inputs are numbers, use DATE; if they're text, use DATEVALUE.

cols: Yes — DATE(2026,13,1) rolls to Jan 2027; day 0 = last of prev month
Yes — "03/04/2026" depends on the machine's date order
The text isn't a recognizable date -> #VALUE!

when.use_when: Assembling dates from parts you already have as numbers: first-of-month (DATE(YEAR(A2),MONTH(A2),1)), shifting years, or turning three columns (Y/M/D) into one date. Its roll-over behavior also powers month-end and next-anniversary tricks.

Fixing dates that arrived as TEXT — CSV imports, pasted logs, ISO strings — so they sort and calculate. Prefer unambiguous ISO (yyyy-mm-dd) input; locale-order strings like 03/04/2026 can be misread as March 4 or April 3.

compat_note: Both execute correctly in every LibreOffice version we test (DATE(2026,7,21) and DATEVALUE("2026-07-21") both return the same serial in LibreOffice; Google Sheets executed 2026-08-29 and Excel for the web executed 2026-09-01 both match, every case; desktop Excel per documentation). DATEVALUE parses time-less date strings; its sibling TIMEVALUE parses times, and combining them reconstructs a full timestamp from text. The reverse direction — a real date to formatted text — is TEXT.
